Edge 1–2 is in two snapshots, so it is ink. union_all merges nodes by id and keeps every edge: the path 1–2–3–4 with 3 edges, each in the color of the snapshot it came from." width="100%"} Applies `union()` from left to right: nodes with the same ID are merged, and every edge of every graph is kept (edges joining the same pair of IDs are merged). Use it to combine several snapshots or layers that share a node numbering into one graph. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [graphs]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A non-empty list of graphs with the same directedness. None is modified. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph (a copy, if only one graph is given). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the list is empty or the graphs differ in directedness. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Equivalent to `graphs[0].union(graphs[1]).union(graphs[2])...`, so where graphs disagree on a label or attribute, the earlier graph wins as described in `union()`. Mirrors NetworkX's `union_all`, except that NetworkX requires disjoint node sets while EdgeCase merges by ID (use `disjoint_union_all()` to keep graphs apart). ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~union`) : Combine two graphs, matching nodes by ID. [](`~compose_all`) : Apply any number of graphs in order. [](`~intersection_all`) : Keep the edges common to any number of graphs. ## Examples {.doc-examples} `ec.friends()` is a network of friendships among the same 24 people in 2024, and `snapshot=2` gives the network a year later, with 8 new friendships. In 2026 three of the 2025 friendships ended. All three snapshots share their node IDs, so their union holds every friendship of the three years: ::: {#b8288ac6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec years = [ ec.friends(), ec.friends(snapshot=2), ec.friends(snapshot=2) .delete_edge("Dev", "Femi") .delete_edge("Gwen", "Lou") .delete_edge("Rosa", "Sven"), ] [year.count_edges() for year in years] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [43, 51, 48] ``` ::: ::: The three ties lost in 2026 were there in 2024, and the new ones were added in 2025, so the union is the 51 friendships of 2025: ::: {#b3225d40 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} ec.Graph.union_all(years).count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 51 ``` ::: ::: As with `union()`, the first graph's values win where the graphs disagree.
